To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIF-alpha accumulation in polycystin-1 deficient cells is responsible for increased erythropoietine production and pericysts hypervascularity, which may have an impact of the progression of PKD.

the HIF-alpha subunits are up-regulated in human PKD, which may be a consequence of pericystic microhypoxia, and that HIF-1 and HIF-3 may be responsible for the increase of erythropoiesis and angiogenesis, respectively.

the hypoxia-inducing factors (HIF) are up-regulated in polycystin-1-deficient cells and that this up-regulation leads to the increased production of erythropoietine and vascular endothelial growth factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular basis of polycystic disease and its complications.
the molecular mechanisms of the pathogenesis and progression of polycystic disease.
the role of the HIFs and their downstream target genes in the development of PKD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HIF-1 alpha is involved in vascular endothelial cell proliferation and migration in the cystic kidney, whereas HIF-2 alpha is involved in the regulation of erythropoiesis and angiogenesis in the polycystic organ.
HIF-2α is upregulated in cystic epithelium, HIF-1α in cystic stroma, and that both isoforms are responsible for the upregulation of EPO and vascularization.
hypoxic conditions are present in the polycystic organ, and that this may be one of the driving forces of the disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

hypoxia-inducing transcription factor (HIF) accumulation in human and rodent PKD is responsible for increased erythropoietic production and pericysts hypervascularity, which may have an impact in progression of the disease.
hypoxia and HIFs are involved in the development and progression of PKD.
hypoxia-inducing transcription factors are involved in polycystin-deficiency-induced cyst expansion and progression of PKD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypoxia-inducing factors may play an important role in the development of PKD.
HIF-alpha accumulation in polycystin-defective cells may be a consequence of regional hypoxemia, rather than a direct consequence of polycystic disease.
HIF-alpha isoform-specific regulation may be involved in the pathophysiology of PKD and may be a target for therapeutic intervention.
